summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors, and East Nusa Tenggara stands under that national framework with no documented local deviation from it. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising across the country. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him, a claim Indonesian police denied.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. For East Nusa Tenggara specifically, no trans-specific statute, raid or service record is documented, so a visitor should expect the national pattern of selective prosecution, police raids on private gatherings and mob violence rather than any province-specific regime.
tangentialFactors:
Aceh is the only province enforcing sharia-based criminalisation of same-sex activity, which means a visitor moving between provinces faces a materially different legal picture; East Nusa Tenggara is not among the provinces with local criminalising provisions.

Nationally, private same-sex activity is not punished outside the new extra-marital sex provision and the two exceptional provinces, yet three men were arrested in August 2025 over an alleged LGBTQ Facebook community page and face up to 12 years' imprisonment if convicted, showing that online association can draw charges even where private conduct is not targeted.

East Nusa Tenggara is a strongly Christian-majority province. Religion-based moral policing is therefore unlikely to operate there in the Aceh model, but the national penal code, the pornography law and police morality enforcement apply regardless of local religious composition.

The absence of any national-level protection against discrimination is the operative baseline a visitor to the province stands under: there is no statutory complaint route if an airline, hotel, clinic or employer refuses service on grounds of gender identity.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change on official documents requires sex-reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval, and identity documents carry only 'male' or 'female' with no third-gender or X marker available.

No trans-specific statute, raid or service record exists for East Nusa Tenggara, so no local divergence from the national baseline is documented either way; residents and local organisations operate under the national penal code, the 2006 pornography law and the absence of anti-discrimination and hate-crime protections for sexual orientation or gender identity.

Local residents live under the same presidential decree of October 2025 that frames LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat, and under the same risk of vigilante attack reported elsewhere in Indonesia.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no source on how the 2 January 2026 penal-code provision has been enforced in East Nusa Tenggara, whether any arrests under it have occurred in the province, or whether local police have conducted raids there. The claim that no trans-specific statute, raid or service record is documented rests on the absence of record in the available sources, not on a positive finding that none exists.

Sources on local bylaws, provincial regulations or regional police directives applicable in East Nusa Tenggara were not available for this pass, so the presence or absence of sub-national morality provisions beyond the Aceh and South Sumatra cases is unresolved.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, HIV services and legal aid in the province is not sourced here. Whether the province's hospitals perform the surgical assessment required for legal gender recognition, and whether any local civil-society group assists trans residents, remain unsourced.
